https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/vulcan-st.plain_summary: Vulcan Energy is building a 30-megawatt (MW) geothermal power plant in Landau, Germany that will extract heat from hot rocks deep underground to generate electricity and heat. The facility, part of a larger project called Lionheart, will also extract lithium (a valuable mineral used in batteries) from hot mineral-rich water that comes up from the same deep wells, making it a combined energy and mineral extraction operation. Early construction work on foundations and roads has started, with full construction expected to begin by 2027.
key_figures: 24,000 tonnes lithium hydroxide monohydrate annual target
second drilling site operational by mid-2026

https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/5-mw-geot.title: 5-MW geothermal pilot project in Meshginshahr, Iran starts grid supply
https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/5-mw-geot.plain_summary: Iran has successfully started operating its first geothermal power plant in Meshginshahr, which generates 5.4 megawatts of electricity by harnessing heat from deep underground rock. The plant taps into a geothermal reservoir (hot rock formations beneath the surface) estimated to hold enough energy for 250 megawatts total, with wells drilled to depths of 3,000 meters already capable of supporting 30 megawatts of production. After decades of planning and exploration starting in 1975, this pilot project represents a major milestone for Iran's renewable energy development.

https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/drilling-.title: Drilling of geothermal research well starts in Cologne-Dellbrück, Germany
https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/drilling-.plain_summary: Germany has begun drilling an exploratory well in Cologne to test whether limestone layers deep underground can be used as geothermal reservoirs (natural underground storage areas for hot water). Researchers will drill down to 1,000 meters and collect rock samples to check if the limestone contains natural cavities and cracks that could hold warm water suitable for heating. The data gathered will help municipalities across the region understand whether they can tap into geothermal energy resources beneath their communities.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Field demonstration and integrated productivity-economics assessment of multi-lateral geothermal wells enabled by directional steel shot drilling
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: Researchers conducted a real-world test of geothermal wells that branch out in multiple directions underground (called multi-lateral wells) using a specialized drilling technique with steel shot pellets instead of traditional drill bits. The study examined whether this directional drilling approach works effectively and whether it makes economic sense financially for geothermal energy production.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Influence of fluid-rock interactions on mechanical, thermal and transport properties of sandstone reservoir during geothermal waste fluid reinjection
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: Researchers studied how hot geothermal fluids (water heated by Earth's interior) interact with sandstone rock when pumped back underground after energy extraction, focusing on how these interactions change the rock's strength, heat capacity, and ability to allow fluid flow. Understanding these changes is important for superhot rock geothermal systems that rely on reinjecting cooled fluids to maintain long-term productivity and prevent damage to the reservoir.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Experimental study of anisotropic behavior of biotite-ordered granite under thermally-coupled true triaxial compression conditions in deep geothermal boreholes
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: Researchers studied how granite rock behaves when exposed to extreme heat and pressure deep underground, similar to conditions found in geothermal boreholes (holes drilled into the earth to access hot rock). They focused on biotite-ordered granite (a type of crystalline rock containing the mineral biotite) and tested how it responds differently depending on the direction of applied forces, which is important for understanding rock stability during superhot rock geothermal drilling and extraction.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Thermo-hydraulic drivers of superhot geothermal well performance
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: This research article examines how heat and fluid flow work together to affect how superhot geothermal wells (wells drilled into extremely hot underground rock) perform. The study, published in a peer-reviewed geothermal journal, explores the technical factors that determine whether these high-temperature wells can effectively extract energy from deep underground.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Damage evolution of thermal shock in granite for enhanced geothermal systems
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: Researchers studied how granite rock breaks down when exposed to repeated heating and cooling cycles, which is important for enhanced geothermal systems (engineered reservoirs created by fracturing hot rock underground to extract heat). Understanding this damage process helps engineers design better methods to create and maintain the fractures needed to circulate water through superhot rock and generate electricity.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Machine learning-driven optimization of production-injection scheme: A case study of geothermal doublet system in Yangling, Guanzhong Basin
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: Researchers used artificial intelligence (a computer system that learns from data) to improve how geothermal energy is extracted from hot rock formations in China. They studied a geothermal doublet system—two connected wells where hot water is pumped from one well and cooler water is returned through another—to figure out the best way to produce energy while keeping the system running efficiently over time.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Sustainable cementitious blends incorporating rice husk ash and silica flour for geothermal well applications
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: Researchers have developed new types of cement blends using rice husk ash (a byproduct from rice processing) and silica flour (a fine mineral powder) that are designed to work better in geothermal wells, which are boreholes drilled deep into the Earth to access heat. These sustainable cement mixtures could improve the durability and performance of well construction in high-temperature geothermal environments.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Liquid nitrogen as a waterless fracturing fluid for enhanced geothermal systems: Mechanisms, challenges, and opportunities
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: Researchers are studying how liquid nitrogen (extremely cold nitrogen in liquid form) could be used instead of water to crack rock deep underground for enhanced geothermal systems (EGS), which are engineered reservoirs designed to extract heat from hot rock). The article examines how this waterless approach works, what problems might arise, and what potential benefits it could offer for superhot rock geothermal energy development.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Advancing geothermal reservoir temperature prediction in the Western Anatolia (Türkiye) using synthetic hydrogeochemical data from rank–Gaussian copulas
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: Researchers in Turkey have developed a new method to predict how hot geothermal reservoirs (underground areas containing hot water and steam) actually are by using synthetic hydrogeochemical data—information about the chemical makeup of fluids in the ground created through statistical modeling. This technique could help geothermal energy developers better understand subsurface conditions in Western Anatolia before drilling, making projects more efficient.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Preliminary Assessment of CO<sub>2</sub> Compression Behavior Modified by [BMIM][AlCl<sub>4</sub>] for Engineered Geothermal Working Fluids
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: Researchers studied how a special chemical compound affects the behavior of carbon dioxide (CO₂) when it is compressed and used as a working fluid in engineered geothermal systems. Working fluids are substances that transfer heat from hot rocks to generate power. This research explores whether modified CO₂ could improve the efficiency of geothermal energy extraction from superhot rock reservoirs.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: The potential for supercritical geothermal resources in the Taupō Volcanic Zone
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: Researchers have published a study examining supercritical geothermal resources (extremely hot, high-pressure underground fluids that can generate large amounts of energy) in New Zealand's Taupō Volcanic Zone. The study explores the potential of this region to support advanced geothermal energy development by analyzing the underground conditions that could make such projects viable.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Thermal depletion patterns of CO<sub>2</sub> and water in closed-loop coaxial geothermal systems with vertical and L-shaped wells
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: This research paper examines how heat is lost over time in closed-loop geothermal systems (systems where fluid circulates continuously underground without escaping) that use either straight vertical wells or L-shaped wells. The study compares how two different heat transfer fluids—carbon dioxide and water—perform in these configurations, helping engineers understand which well designs and fluids are most efficient for extracting heat from hot rock over extended periods.

https://www.geothermalcanada.org/news/20.title: Eavor hopes drilling tech means geothermal deeper, hotter, anywhere
https://www.geothermalcanada.org/news/20.plain_summary: Eavor Technologies is developing a new drilling technology called Eavor-Jules that would allow geothermal systems (which extract heat from hot rocks underground) to operate much deeper and access significantly hotter temperatures. The technology could reach depths of 15 kilometers where temperatures exceed 400°C, making it possible to generate more electricity and heat from each system while reducing costs and enabling geothermal projects in regions worldwide that currently aren't suitable for this type of energy.

https://www.geothermalcanada.org/news/20.title: Rodatherm partners with Fulcrum Point for closed-loop geothermal pilot in Utah
https://www.geothermalcanada.org/news/20.plain_summary: Two energy companies are teaming up to build geothermal power plants in Utah using closed-loop technology, which means hot water or special fluids circulate in sealed pipes underground to generate electricity without losing water to evaporation. Their initial project aims to produce 10 megawatts of power (enough for thousands of homes), with plans to eventually expand to 200 megawatts. Rodatherm's proprietary system uses an organic working fluid instead of water and claims to be 50% more efficient than traditional geothermal methods while costing less to operate and maintain.
key_figures: $8 million grant from Emissions Reduction Alberta

https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/geophysic.title: Geophysical measurements completed by ENNA at Babina Greda geothermal site, Croatia
https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/geophysic.plain_summary: A geothermal energy company completed detailed underground imaging surveys at a geothermal site in Croatia to better understand the heat potential of the area. These surveys used two types of measurements—3D seismic (sound wave mapping) and magnetotelluric (measuring natural electromagnetic fields)—to create a picture of the underground geothermal reservoir. The company plans to use this information to plan future drilling and development of the geothermal fields.

https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/construct.title: Construction of geothermal heating plant in Sochaczew, Poland nears completion
https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/construct.plain_summary: A geothermal heating plant in Sochaczew, Poland is almost finished being built and will soon start operating. The plant uses heat pumps (devices that move heat from one place to another) and geothermal wells (deep holes that access naturally hot water underground) to provide about 40% of the city's heating from renewable sources, with backup boilers for extremely cold weather. Two wells have been drilled to depths over 1,600 meters, and the system is being funded through a major government grant.
key_figures: PLN 62 million (USD 15.63 million) total project funding

https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/yeager-en.title: Yeager Energy expands geothermal business in Netherlands with third acquisition
https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/yeager-en.plain_summary: Yeager Energy, a company developing geothermal projects (systems that use heat from deep underground rock), has acquired a third geothermal greenhouse company in the Netherlands called Aardwarmte Vierpolders. The company now operates four geothermal projects with a total heat output of 60 MWth (megawatts of thermal energy) and is developing five additional projects to supply heat to greenhouses, homes, and industries across Europe.
key_figures: €100 million funding from Pioneer Point Partners

https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/elc-elect.title: ELC Electroconsult awarded drilling supervision contract for Ngozi geothermal project, Tanzania
https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/elc-elect.plain_summary: An Italian consulting company has been hired to supervise exploratory drilling at a geothermal project in Tanzania called Ngozi. They will oversee the drilling of three slim wells (smaller-diameter wells used for initial exploration) and help train local technical staff in drilling and reservoir skills. The information gathered from these wells will help determine if Ngozi can contribute to Tanzania's goal of generating over 200 MW (megawatts, a unit of power) from geothermal sources.
key_figures: 200 MW geothermal power generation capacity target for Tanzania

https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/universit.title: Universities in Aberdeen, UK partner for collaboration opportunities in geothermal
https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/universit.plain_summary: Two Scottish universities have partnered to explore geothermal energy opportunities, which is technology that uses heat from deep underground rock to provide heating while reducing carbon emissions. Their collaboration will focus on research, training, and funding to develop geothermal projects in the UK, with one university recently receiving support to study whether Aberdeen could use this technology for heating.
key_figures: £1 million grant for Aberdeen Geothermal Feasibility Pilot in 2025

https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/the-azore.title: The Azores will host the second edition of Geo-RIN 2027
https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/the-azore.plain_summary: The Azores in Portugal will host a major geothermal energy conference in March 2027 that brings together researchers and companies from Spain and Portugal to discuss geothermal technology and innovation. The conference will cover various geothermal systems (both shallow and deep underground heat sources), next-generation technologies like Enhanced Geothermal Systems (engineered reservoirs created by fracturing hot rock), and how geothermal energy can be integrated into cities and industry. Registration is now open and researchers can submit abstracts of their work until October 2026.

https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/pertamina.title: Pertamina Geothermal secures $75 m financing from Mizuho
https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/pertamina.plain_summary: An Indonesian geothermal company called Pertamina Geothermal Energy has received $75 million in financing from a Japanese bank to support its operations and future projects. The company plans to use this funding along with other recent investments to expand its geothermal capacity (the amount of electricity it can generate) significantly over the next decade.
key_figures: $477.87 million prior financing from JICA and World Bank

https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/badenova-.title: Badenova, Herrenknecht finalize joint geothermal project in Hartheim, Germany
https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/badenova-.plain_summary: Two German companies are partnering to build a deep geothermal heating project near Freiburg that will tap into hot rock layers approximately 3.2 kilometers underground to provide heat to around 2,000 homes. Deep geothermal energy involves drilling deep wells to access naturally hot rock formations (rather than using fossil fuels) to generate sustainable heat. The project received regulatory approval and is expected to begin drilling in late 2027.
key_figures: 2000 households to be supplied with heat

https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/registrat.title: Registration open – 11th African Rift Geothermal Conference; 19-24 October 2026; Comoros
https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/registrat.plain_summary: A major conference on geothermal energy in Africa is accepting registrations for October 2026 in Comoros. The event will bring together experts, policymakers, and investors to discuss how African countries can develop their geothermal resources (heat energy from within the Earth) for electricity generation and sustainable development. The program covers geology, drilling technology, power plant design, financing, and environmental concerns.
key_figures: 12 additional countries represented at previous edition

https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/undergrou.title: Underground heat storage pilot in Bern, Switzerland progresses with test drilling
https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/undergrou.plain_summary: A pilot project in Switzerland is testing underground heat storage using geothermal probes (pipes that exchange heat with the ground). The system will capture excess heat from a waste incineration plant during summer and store it deep underground, then retrieve it in winter to heat homes through a district heating network. Early testing has involved drilling to 400 meters depth and installing five test probes to measure how well heat conducts through the rock and soil.

https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/philippin.title: Philippine economy council approves $170m geothermal de-risking facility
https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/philippin.plain_summary: The Philippines has approved a $170 million government fund to help reduce financial risk for companies exploring geothermal energy (heat from within the Earth used to generate electricity). The fund will cover at least half the costs of geothermal drilling and exploration, with companies only repaying the government if their exploration finds economically viable resources. This initiative aims to boost geothermal development in the Philippines, which currently ranks third globally in geothermal power capacity but has seen slower growth compared to neighboring countries.
key_figures: 50% cost coverage for exploration and drilling
3rd global ranking in installed geothermal capacity

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: A GIS-based geothermal heat cost index (GHCI) map for efficient energy planning in Europe
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: Researchers have created a digital map tool that shows where geothermal heat energy is most cost-effective across Europe. This mapping system helps cities and regions plan where to invest in geothermal projects by analyzing the expenses involved in tapping heat from underground rocks.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Uncertainty quantification under data worth for the Delft campus geothermal project
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: Researchers at Delft University studied how to measure and reduce uncertainty when deciding what data to collect for a geothermal project on their campus. They used statistical methods to figure out which measurements would be most valuable for understanding the subsurface (the rock layers below ground) and improving predictions about the geothermal system's performance.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Thermal structure and geothermal potential of the onshore Gippsland basin inferred from 3D conductive heat flow modelling
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: Researchers used computer models to map underground heat distribution in Australia's Gippsland basin to assess how much geothermal energy could be extracted there. By simulating heat flow through rock layers in three dimensions, they identified areas with the highest potential for developing geothermal resources in this region.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Quantifying geothermal heat loss at the Dayoukeng crater using UAV thermal imaging and comparison with Landsat-derived estimates
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: Researchers used drone thermal imaging technology to measure heat being lost from the Dayoukeng crater, a geothermal feature, and compared their findings with satellite data from Landsat. This study helps scientists better understand and quantify the amount of thermal energy naturally radiating from geothermal sites, which is important for assessing geothermal resources.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Nigorikawa and Otake – Pioneering geothermal binary plants in Japan: Historical perspective, performance assessment, and lessons learned
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: This academic article examines two pioneering geothermal power plants in Japan—Nigorikawa and Otake—that used binary cycle technology (a system where hot geothermal fluid heats a separate working fluid to spin turbines). The paper reviews their historical development, analyzes how well they performed over time, and discusses what lessons the geothermal industry can learn from their successes and challenges.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Integrated geothermometry for mixed-fluid carbonate geothermal systems under structural and hydrochemical constraints: Insights from the Yichuan Basin, central China
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: Researchers studied how to measure underground temperatures in geothermal systems located in China's Yichuan Basin, where hot water and other fluids mix together in carbonate rock formations (porous rocks made of calcium compounds). They developed improved methods to accurately determine subsurface temperatures by considering both the rock structure and the chemical composition of fluids, which helps better understand geothermal reservoirs.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Limited heat connectivity across the Northeastern Segment of the Tanlu Fault, China: Implications for low–temperature geothermal systems
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: Researchers studied the Tanlu Fault in northeastern China and found that heat does not flow uniformly across this geological feature, which has important consequences for developing low-temperature geothermal systems (operations that extract warmth from relatively cool underground areas) in the region. Understanding how heat moves through faults is essential for identifying the best locations to build geothermal energy projects.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Distribution characteristics and controlling factors of the thermal field and geothermal resource potential on the southern margin of the Junggar basin
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: Researchers studied the heat distribution and geothermal potential in the southern part of the Junggar Basin, a geological region that could be suitable for extracting energy from hot rock underground. The study identifies where the hottest rock layers are located and what natural factors control these temperature patterns, which is important information for planning future geothermal energy projects in that area.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Potential assessment of critical raw materials from European geothermal fluids
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: Researchers are studying whether geothermal fluids—the hot water and steam that comes up from deep underground in geothermal systems—could be a source of valuable rare materials needed for electronics and other technologies. This European research explores extracting critical raw materials (like metals) from geothermal fluids, which could provide an additional economic benefit beyond just generating heat and electricity.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Field-validated thermodynamic assessment of hybrid gas-removal systems for geothermal power plants
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: Researchers tested hybrid gas-removal systems (equipment that takes out unwanted gases) at real geothermal power plants to evaluate how well they work from a thermodynamic perspective (how efficiently they use heat energy). This study helps improve the performance and reliability of geothermal facilities that generate electricity from heat beneath the Earth's surface.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Tracing the source and evolution of organic matter in geothermal environments
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: Scientists studied how organic matter (carbon-based materials from living things and their remnants) changes and moves in geothermal environments where hot rock underground is used for energy. This research helps understand what happens to biological materials when they're exposed to the extreme heat and pressure found deep below the Earth's surface in geothermal systems.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Geochemical dynamics and predictive modeling of water-rock interaction during geothermal reinjection in coal mine gobs
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: Researchers studied how water and rock interact chemically when hot water is pumped back into abandoned coal mines for geothermal energy production. The study uses computer models to predict what happens underground when reinjection (returning used geothermal fluid) occurs in these mine spaces, helping engineers understand whether this approach could work safely and efficiently.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Optimization of well patterns for heat recovery in sedimentary geothermal systems: A hybrid GRA-COBRA approach
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: Researchers developed a new method to figure out the best way to arrange multiple wells in sedimentary geothermal systems (rock layers underground containing heat and water) to pull out heat most efficiently. The hybrid GRA-COBRA approach combines two different optimization techniques to help engineers decide where to place wells for better heat extraction performance.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Dual-porosity numerical modeling and probabilistic resource assessment of the Ulumbu geothermal field, Flores, Indonesia
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: Researchers created a computer model of the Ulumbu geothermal field in Indonesia using dual-porosity modeling, which accounts for how fluids move through rock with two different types of pore spaces (tiny connected holes). The study assessed the probable amount of geothermal energy resources available at this location, helping determine whether it's viable for energy production.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Unraveling the fluid origin, circulation and heat sources of the fault-controlled Santa Teresita Geothermal System (Pipanaco basin, NW Argentina): insights from hydrochemical, isotopic and structural analysis
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: Researchers studied a geothermal system in Argentina to understand where its hot water comes from, how it moves through the ground, and what heats it up. They used chemical analysis of the water, isotope tracking (measuring different forms of atoms to trace water origins), and structural geology (studying rock formations and faults—cracks in the earth) to map out the system's behavior.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Field to laboratory assessment of subsurface thermal conductivity: A geothermal case study in Slovenia
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: Researchers in Slovenia studied how well heat moves through underground rock layers by comparing measurements taken directly in the field with tests done in laboratory settings. This work helps geothermal energy projects understand the thermal properties (how heat conducts through rock) of the subsurface, which is essential for designing effective geothermal systems that extract heat from deep underground.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Detecting and characterizing a hidden geothermal system in the Mt. Endut area, Indonesia, through integrated soil-gas component analyses
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: Researchers in Indonesia used chemical analysis of gases naturally escaping from soil to discover and map a hidden geothermal system (an underground heat source) beneath Mt. Endut. By examining the composition of these soil gases, scientists were able to characterize the location and properties of this previously unknown thermal resource.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Integrating microbial induced calcium carbonate precipitation (MICP) in geothermal pavements: A coupled thermo-economic numerical evaluation
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: Researchers are studying a way to strengthen geothermal pavements (road surfaces heated by underground thermal energy) by using microorganisms to produce calcium carbonate, a natural cement-like substance. The study analyzes both the thermal performance (heat management) and economic costs of this biological strengthening method to see if it makes sense for real-world geothermal heating systems built into roads.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Geothermal exploration of the Yala River segment of the Xianshuihe Fault Zone, eastern Tibetan Plateau: Insights from CSAMT surveys and deep drilling
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: Researchers used advanced electromagnetic surveys (a technique that maps underground rock structures by measuring electrical properties) and deep drilling to explore geothermal potential in a fault zone on the eastern Tibetan Plateau. This work aimed to identify promising locations for geothermal energy development by understanding the subsurface geology and heat sources in the region.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: High-temperature magmatic-hydrothermal systems inferred by fumarolic fluids from Callaqui volcano, Biobio region, Chile
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: Scientists studied hot volcanic gases released from Callaqui volcano in Chile to understand the deep underground systems where extremely hot water and rock interact with magma (molten rock beneath Earth's surface). By analyzing the chemical composition of these gases, researchers can infer what conditions exist deep below the volcano, which helps identify potential locations for superhot rock geothermal energy development.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Petrologic and geochemical exploration of the plumbing systems under submarine volcanoes Edifice C, Three Sisters and Orca (Bransfield Strait, Antarctica)
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: This research examines the internal rock and chemical composition of underwater volcanoes in Antarctica to understand how hot fluids and magma (molten rock) move through the ground beneath them. By studying these natural volcanic systems, scientists gain insights into the subsurface structures and processes that could inform development of superhot rock geothermal energy, which harnesses extreme heat from deep underground.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Laboratory observations of elasto-acoustic signals of rock fragmentation, fluid-filled cavities formation, stick-slip motion and mass flux dynamics
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: This scientific study examines acoustic signals (sound waves produced by rock stress) that occur when rocks break apart, when fluid-filled spaces form inside rocks, and when friction causes stick-slip motion (sudden jerky movement along surfaces). The research helps understand the physical processes happening deep underground during geothermal operations by analyzing these signals in laboratory experiments.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Hydrothermal alteration facies model and its link to rock mechanics - A comparative analysis of andesitic volcanoes in New Zealand
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: This research examines how volcanic rocks in New Zealand change their physical properties when exposed to hot, mineral-rich fluids underground—a process called hydrothermal alteration. The study compares how these chemical changes affect the mechanical strength and behavior of andesite rock (a common volcanic rock type), which is important for understanding how rocks behave at depth in geothermal systems.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Alteration pathways of the Serra Geral Group basalts and their controls on the petrophysical properties of volcanic reservoirs
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: This research examines how volcanic rock from the Serra Geral Group breaks down and changes over time, and how these changes affect the rock's ability to store and transmit fluids—properties crucial for using volcanic reservoirs as geothermal resources. The study identifies the specific pathways through which these basalt rocks (a type of volcanic rock) transform and explains what controls these transformations, providing insights relevant to developing geothermal energy in volcanic regions.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: The Rotokawa geothermal system, New Zealand: Hydrothermal minerals and punctuated evolution
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: This academic paper examines the Rotokawa geothermal system in New Zealand, focusing on the minerals formed by hot water moving through rock and how the system has changed over time through distinct evolutionary phases. Understanding these mineral deposits and system changes helps researchers better characterize geothermal reservoirs.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Isotopic evidence for slab-derived magmatic water beneath the Kussharo Caldera, Japan
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: Researchers studying the Kussharo Caldera in Japan found chemical evidence that water trapped in the deep rock layers comes from subducting oceanic plates (slabs of Earth's crust sinking into the mantle). This discovery helps scientists understand how water moves through volcanic regions and could inform geothermal energy exploration by revealing where hot water resources exist underground.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Geo-THM characterization for safe CO<sub>2</sub> storage and geothermal energy in karstified-fractured carbonates: A reservoir and geomechanical risk management framework
Modelling hot water and power production from a low-enthalpy geothermal carbonate reservoir; South Swan Hills, Alberta, Canada
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: Researchers studied how to extract heat and generate electricity from a warm rock reservoir in Alberta, Canada that contains carbonate rock (a type of rock made from calcium-based minerals). The project models whether this lower-temperature geothermal resource could be practical for power production, focusing on understanding the underground conditions that affect how much hot water can be pumped out and used.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Transient thermal performance of U-loop geothermal systems with dual-borehole lateral sections using a computationally efficient framework
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: Researchers developed a fast computer model to predict how U-shaped pipes (a common underground heat exchange design where pipes loop down and back up) perform when they have two boreholes—holes drilled into the ground—with horizontal sections extending sideways. This model helps engineers understand how temperature changes over time in these geothermal systems, which is important for designing efficient heating and cooling systems that use Earth's heat.

https://www.edengeothermal.com/2026/07/2.title: Eden Geothermal Speaks at Kings College London
https://www.edengeothermal.com/2026/07/2.plain_summary: Eden Geothermal participated in a speaking event at King's College London focused on how to gain public support for deep geothermal energy projects (energy extracted from hot rock deep underground). The company shared lessons learned from their own geothermal project and discussed findings about public perceptions of this technology, alongside other experts in the field.
